To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a pseudopeptide receptor containing an acridinium unit has a selective fluorescence response to free tryptophane in water under acidic conditions.
the fluorescence of a pseudopeptide receptor is quenched by free tryptophane in water, and that the quenching is selective and is due to the formation of a supramolecular complex.

the prepared pseudopeptide receptors show a fluorescence response to tryptopan in water and that this response is based on the formation of an aromatic-aromatic association that is assisted by the presence of hydrogen sulfate anions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of synthetic receptors that are able to recognize amino acids in water, a challenging task in supramolecular chemistry.
the development of a novel class of pseudopeptidic receptor molecules able to recognize Trp in aqueous solution.
the design of a new family of pseudopeptidic fluorescent receptors that are selective towards Trp in water.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pseudopeptidic receptor is capable of recognizing the indole moiety of the Trp side chain, and that this recognition process is facilitated by the presence of a hydrogen sulfate anion.

the receptor is able to discriminate Trp from the other amino acids by a combination of the following factors: (i) a favorable electrostatic interaction between the cationic groups of both the receptor and the amino acid, (ii) a specific interaction between the indole and the acridine moieties of the supramolecular complex and (iii) a specific interaction of the cations with hydrogen sulfate anion.

the pseudopeptide receptors are selective for free Trp in water, and the selectivity is based on the existence in solution of supramolecular complexes formed by the receptor and the amino acid that involve the indole ring, the acridinium unit, and the anions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have designed and developed a synthetic receptor that is able to recognize Trp, a biologically relevant amino acid that is present in proteins and peptides.
the receptor displays a selective fluorescence response to free Trp in water, and this response is enhanced by the macrocyclic nature and by the protonated form of the receptors.
the recognition of free tryptanthine (Trp) in water is possible using a pseudopeptide receptor containing an acridinium moiety.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, under the experimental conditions used, the fluorescence response of the receptors is not only a function of the size of the amino acid but also of the chemical nature of its side chain.
the use of free amino acids in water is a valid approach to the study of pseudopeptidic receptor-guest recognition.

the use of pseudopeptide-based receptors containing a fluorescent unit is an effective strategy for the recognition of free amino acids in water, which can be used as a starting point to develop fluorescent probes for the detection of free amino acids.
